quests.hint: A shared situation is the easiest opening: comment on it, then ask a light question.
quests.explanation: Talking to strangers usually begins with something you both experience, like the weather. The comment gives the other person something to agree with, and the question invites them to keep talking.
quests.situationText: Rain is pouring down at a bus stop and the bus is late. The woman next to you keeps checking her watch too.
quests.sampleAnswer: This rain is terrible, isn't it? Have you been waiting long?
quests.correctAnswer: Looks like the rain isn't stopping. Have you been waiting long?
acceptedSynonyms: Looks like the rain isn't stopping. Have you been waiting long?
The bus is really late today. Have you been here long?
It's pouring, isn't it? Are you waiting for the bus as well?
What awful weather. How long have you been standing here?

quests.hint: At an event, ask about the person's connection to it. Say your name so the exchange is mutual.
quests.explanation: 'Is this your first time?' works at any event because everyone has an answer. Giving your name first makes it a real introduction and not an interview.
quests.situationText: During a coffee break at a professional conference, you notice a man next to you wearing a badge with the name Marco. Your name is Kenji.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi there, Kenji here. Are you enjoying the event so far?
quests.correctAnswer: Hi, I'm Kenji. Is this your first time at this event?
acceptedSynonyms: Hello, I'm Kenji. Have you been to this conference before?
Hi there, Kenji here. Are you enjoying the event so far?
Hi, I'm Kenji. Is this your first time at this event?
I don't think we've met. I'm Kenji. Is this your first year here?

quests.hint: Comments about a pet break the ice easily. Compliment and ask the name.
quests.explanation: People love talking about their pets, so a compliment plus a question about the name is almost guaranteed to start a friendly chat.
quests.situationText: In a local park, a small brown dog runs up and sniffs your shoes while its owner walks over, smiling.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, hello! What a lovely dog. What's his name?
quests.correctAnswer: Your dog is so friendly! What's his name?
acceptedSynonyms: Your dog is so friendly! What's his name?
He's adorable! What's he called?
What a sweet dog. Is it a he or a she, and what's the name?
Aw, he's so friendly. What's his name?

quests.hint: Show interest in the reason behind what the other person said. 'What made you…?' asks for a story.
quests.explanation: 'What made you…?' invites a longer answer than a yes/no question. It signals that you're interested in the person, not just the fact.
quests.situationText: Your new coworker mentions she moved to your city from Lisbon last spring. You're curious.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, that's a big change! What made you move here?
quests.correctAnswer: Oh, nice! What made you decide to move here?
acceptedSynonyms: Really? What brought you here from Lisbon?
That's interesting. Why did you choose this city?
Oh, nice! What made you decide to move here?
Oh wow. What made you leave Lisbon?

quests.hint: React to the news, then ask an open question about the experience.
quests.explanation: An open question like 'What was the best part?' gets a story. A reaction first, like 'Oh, lucky you', shows you care about their experience.
quests.situationText: Your friend just got back from a two-week trip to Japan and is showing you photos on his phone.
quests.sampleAnswer: Wow, these are great photos! What was the best part of the trip?
quests.correctAnswer: How was it? What was the best part?
acceptedSynonyms: How was it? What was the best part?
Lucky you! What did you enjoy most?
These look amazing. What was your favorite place?
That looks incredible. What was the highlight for you?

quests.hint: Admire what the person does, then ask something practical that shows real interest.
quests.explanation: Practical questions such as how someone finds the time show that you're thinking about their experience. It's more engaging than a generic 'that's nice'.
quests.situationText: At a party, a woman mentions that she runs marathons and trains before work every morning. You've never run more than a mile.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's amazing. I could never do that! How do you find time to train?
quests.correctAnswer: Wow, that's impressive. How do you find the time to train?
acceptedSynonyms: That sounds tough! How do you fit the training in?
I'm impressed. When do you manage to train with a busy schedule?
Wow, that's impressive. How do you find the time to train?
Really? How did you get into running marathons?

quests.hint: Use the past tense for what happened, and add a place and an activity. Details make a story.
quests.explanation: A weekend story needs two or three concrete details: the place, the day, what you did. Vague answers like 'It was good' end the conversation early.
quests.situationText: On Monday morning, a coworker asks, 'Did you do anything nice at the weekend?' You drove to the coast on Saturday and had lunch by the sea.
quests.sampleAnswer: I did, actually. We took a trip to the coast and had lunch by the sea.
quests.correctAnswer: It was great. We drove to the coast on Saturday and had lunch by the sea.
acceptedSynonyms: Yes, we went to the coast on Saturday. We had lunch right by the sea.
Pretty good, thanks. On Saturday we drove out to the coast and ate by the sea.
I did, actually. We took a trip to the coast and had lunch by the sea.
It was great. We drove to the coast on Saturday and had lunch by the sea.

quests.hint: A story often has a good part and a but. Use 'but' to show the twist.
quests.explanation: Using 'but' gives your story a twist and makes it feel real. Sequencing in the past tense (arrived late, missed the first song) helps listeners follow.
quests.situationText: Your friend asks how the concert was. The music was fantastic, but you got there late and missed the opening song.
quests.sampleAnswer: It was fantastic, but we arrived late and missed the first song.
quests.correctAnswer: The concert was fantastic, but we got there late and missed the first song.
acceptedSynonyms: It was amazing, although we were late and we missed the first song.
The concert was fantastic, but we got there late and missed the first song.
Really good! We got there late, though, so we missed the opening song.
Honestly, it was brilliant, but we missed the first song because we arrived late.

quests.hint: Use 'then' and 'so' to link events in order. It turns a list of bad things into a story.
quests.explanation: 'Then' shows sequence and 'so' shows result. Linking words make a spoken story easy to follow, and they're more natural than a list of short sentences.
quests.situationText: Your friend asks why you look so tired at lunch. Your morning was chaotic: you missed the bus, spilled coffee on your shirt, and arrived late.
quests.sampleAnswer: Don't ask. I missed my bus, ruined my shirt with coffee, and got in late as a result.
quests.correctAnswer: I missed my bus, then I spilled coffee on my shirt, so I was late for work.
acceptedSynonyms: It's been a rough day. First I missed the bus, and then coffee went all over my shirt. I got to work late.
My morning was a mess: I missed the bus, spilled coffee on my shirt, and arrived late.
Don't ask. I missed my bus, ruined my shirt with coffee, and got in late as a result.
I missed my bus, then I spilled coffee on my shirt, so I was late for work.

quests.hint: Suggest an activity, then add a reason to make it attractive. 'How about…?' is friendly.
quests.explanation: 'How about…?' offers an idea without pressure. Adding the reason ('the weather looks good') gives the friend something to agree with.
quests.situationText: It's Thursday, the forecast for Saturday is sunny, and your friend Mia has been wanting to get outside.
quests.sampleAnswer: Do you fancy going hiking on Saturday? The weather's meant to be great.
quests.correctAnswer: How about we go hiking on Saturday? The weather looks good.
acceptedSynonyms: What do you think about a hike this Saturday? It's supposed to be sunny.
Shall we go hiking on Saturday? The forecast looks great.
How about we go hiking on Saturday? The weather looks good.
Why don't we go for a hike on Saturday? The weather should be nice.

quests.hint: When you're choosing where to meet, give a time, a place, and a reason.
quests.explanation: A specific meeting time and place removes uncertainty. Adding a reason ('a good pizza place across the road') helps others accept the plan quickly.
quests.situationText: Your friend says, 'Let's have dinner tomorrow, wherever you like.' You'd like to meet near the train station, where there's a pizza place across the road. You want to suggest seven o'clock.
quests.sampleAnswer: How about seven o'clock at the station? There's a nice pizza place opposite.
quests.correctAnswer: Let's meet at seven by the station. There's a good pizza place right across the road.
acceptedSynonyms: Let's meet at seven by the station. There's a good pizza place right across the road.
How about seven o'clock at the station? There's a nice pizza place opposite.
We could meet at the station at seven. There's a great pizza restaurant just across the street.
I'd suggest the station at seven. There's a good pizza place over the road.

quests.hint: In a group chat, offer your own availability instead of asking everyone to guess. It helps the group decide faster.
quests.explanation: Sharing your free times is more useful than asking 'When is everyone free?'. It gives others a starting point and moves the group toward a decision.
quests.situationText: Five friends want to have a birthday dinner together in the next two weeks. In the voice message, you're speaking to the group. You're free on Thursday and Friday evenings.
quests.sampleAnswer: Which day works for everyone? I'm free on Thursday or Friday evening.
quests.correctAnswer: Which day works best for everyone? I'm free on Thursday and Friday evening.
acceptedSynonyms: When can everyone make it? Thursday and Friday evenings are fine for me.
Let's pick a day. I can do Thursday or Friday night. What about you?
Which day works best for everyone? I'm free on Thursday and Friday evening.
What day suits you all? I'm available on Thursday and Friday evening.

quests.hint: Apologize, give a short reason, and propose another time. All three together keep the friendship strong.
quests.explanation: Cancelling without a new suggestion can feel like rejection. Proposing 'next week' shows you still want to meet and makes the apology more meaningful.
quests.situationText: You're supposed to meet your friend Zoe at eight tonight, but you have a fever and you're going to bed. You send her a message.
quests.sampleAnswer: Zoe, I'm really sorry, but I can't come tonight. I'm feeling ill. Could we meet next week instead?
quests.correctAnswer: I'm so sorry, but I can't make it tonight. I'm feeling ill. Can we do it next week?
acceptedSynonyms: I'm sorry, I have to cancel tonight because I'm not well. Can we reschedule for next week?
Really sorry, but I'm not going to be able to come tonight. I've got a fever. How about next week?
Sorry to do this, but I need to cancel. I'm ill. Could we try again next week?
I'm so sorry, but I can't make it tonight. I'm feeling ill. Can we do it next week?

quests.hint: Give the delay and the new time estimate, then say what the others should do.
quests.explanation: When you're late, others want to know two things: how late, and what to do. Telling them to begin without you stops everyone from waiting anxiously.
quests.situationText: You're on your way to a friend's birthday dinner, but the traffic is terrible. You call her from the taxi. You'll be about twenty minutes late.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, the traffic is awful. Give me twenty minutes, and please don't wait for me.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm stuck in traffic and I'll be about twenty minutes late. Please start without me.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm caught in traffic, so I'll be around twenty minutes late. Go ahead and order without me.
I'm stuck in traffic and I'll be about twenty minutes late. Please start without me.
Sorry, the traffic is awful. Give me twenty minutes, and please don't wait for me.
I'm running late because of traffic. It'll be about twenty minutes. Please start eating.

quests.hint: Suggest a change to the group's plan and give the reason. A soft opener like 'Would you mind if…?' works well.
quests.explanation: Changing a plan feels less like a disruption when you ask permission and offer a reason. 'Would you mind if…?' invites agreement instead of announcing a decision.
quests.situationText: You planned to meet friends at a restaurant tonight, but it's raining heavily and no one wants to go out. You send a message to the group.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, can we change our plan? With this rain, how about we stay in and cook at mine?
quests.correctAnswer: Would you mind if we changed the plan? It's raining, so maybe we could just cook at my place.
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, can we change our plan? With this rain, how about we stay in and cook at mine?
Would it be okay to switch plans? It's pouring, so we could have dinner at my place.
What if we didn't go out? The weather's awful, and we could cook at my house.
Would you mind if we changed the plan? It's raining, so maybe we could just cook at my place.

quests.hint: Give the day, time, and place, then ask a direct question to the couple. Include the second person by name.
quests.explanation: Inviting a couple means addressing both of them. Giving the details before the question makes the invitation feel concrete and easy to accept or decline.
quests.situationText: You're inviting your colleague Anna and her husband Tom to a dinner at your home. You meet Anna by the coffee machine. The dinner is next Friday at seven.
quests.sampleAnswer: We're having dinner at our place next Friday at seven. Would you and Tom like to come?
quests.correctAnswer: We're having dinner at our place next Friday at seven. Do you and Tom want to join us?
acceptedSynonyms: We'd love to have you and Tom over for dinner next Friday at seven. Are you free?
We're having dinner at our place next Friday at seven. Do you and Tom want to join us?
I'm cooking dinner at our house next Friday around seven. Would you and Tom like to come?
Next Friday, we're having a few people round for dinner at seven. Can you and Tom make it?

quests.hint: Accept, express thanks, and ask about bringing someone. Two goals in one reply.
quests.explanation: Asking 'Can I bring a guest?' is part of accepting, because it clarifies what the hosts expect. Thanking first shows you value the invitation.
quests.situationText: A colleague has just given you a wedding invitation with a handwritten note. You'd like to go and bring your partner.
quests.sampleAnswer: Thank you so much for inviting me. I'd love to come. Is it okay if I bring my partner?
quests.correctAnswer: Thank you for the invitation! I'd love to come. Can I bring a guest?
acceptedSynonyms: Thanks for inviting me, I'd be happy to attend. May I bring my partner?
That's so kind of you. I'd love to be there. Is my partner invited too?
I'd be delighted to come, thank you. Would it be all right to bring someone?
Thank you for the invitation! I'd love to come. Can I bring a guest?

quests.hint: A last-minute invitation works best when you explain the opportunity and ask casually.
quests.explanation: 'There's a free seat' explains why you're inviting them now and reduces the feeling of being an afterthought. A casual 'Want to come along?' lets them decide easily.
quests.situationText: You and some friends are driving to the beach tomorrow. One friend just cancelled, so you have a free seat and you think of your neighbor Lena.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi Lena, we're driving to the beach tomorrow and we have a free seat. Do you want to come along?
quests.correctAnswer: We're going to the beach tomorrow, and there's a free seat in the car. Want to come along?
acceptedSynonyms: We've got a spare seat in the car for the beach trip tomorrow. Would you like to join us?
We're going to the beach tomorrow, and there's a free seat in the car. Want to come along?
A few of us are heading to the beach tomorrow. There's room for one more, if you're interested.
Someone dropped out of our beach trip tomorrow. Would you like to take the spare seat?

quests.hint: Refuse warmly by agreeing that the idea is good, then give an honest reason and leave the door open.
quests.explanation: 'That sounds fun, but…' respects the offer. Leaving the door open ('maybe another time') tells the friend you value the relationship, not only this invitation.
quests.situationText: A friend invites you to join her gym and try a class together, but you're trying to save money this month.
quests.sampleAnswer: That sounds fun, but I'm trying to save money this month. Maybe another time?
quests.correctAnswer: That sounds fun, but I'm saving money this month. Maybe another time.
acceptedSynonyms: That sounds fun, but I'm saving money this month. Maybe another time.
It's a nice idea, but I'm on a tight budget right now. Let's try it another time.
Thanks for asking, but I can't spend anything extra this month. Maybe later.
I'd love to, but I'm saving up at the moment. Ask me again next month.

quests.hint: You can accept with a limit. State the condition clearly so nobody is surprised.
quests.explanation: Saying you can only stay until ten sets expectations upfront. It's much better than leaving early without explanation, and it lets the host feel you're still enthusiastic.
quests.situationText: A friend invites you to a Friday night party. You'd like to go, but you have a flight at 6 a.m. on Saturday.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'd love to come, but I can only stay until ten because I have an early flight.
quests.correctAnswer: I'd love to come, but I can only stay until ten. I've got an early flight tomorrow.
acceptedSynonyms: Yes, I'll be there, but I'll have to leave by ten. I have a very early flight.
Sounds great. I can come, but only for a couple of hours. My flight is at six in the morning.
I'd love to come, but I can only stay until ten. I've got an early flight tomorrow.
Count me in, but I'll need to go around ten because of my early flight.

quests.hint: Refuse a favor with a sincere regret, then a real reason. 'I wish I could' shows you would help if you could.
quests.explanation: 'I wish I could' signals that your refusal is about circumstances, not unwillingness. A brief true reason makes it easier for the other person to accept.
quests.situationText: A coworker asks you to swap your Sunday shift with his, but you already have plans for that day.
quests.sampleAnswer: I wish I could help, but I already have plans on Sunday. Sorry about that.
quests.correctAnswer: I wish I could, but I already have plans on Sunday. Sorry.
acceptedSynonyms: I wish I could, but I already have plans on Sunday. Sorry.
I'd like to help, but Sunday isn't possible for me. I've already made plans.
Sorry, I can't swap this time. I've got something on Sunday.
Unfortunately, I can't do Sunday. I have plans that I can't change.

quests.hint: Compliment the food and ask a real question about it. Curiosity is a compliment too.
quests.explanation: 'Did you make it yourself?' shows you're impressed and invites a story. Specific praise like this feels more sincere than only saying 'it's good'.
quests.situationText: At a friend's dinner, you taste the lasagna and it's the best you've had in years.
quests.sampleAnswer: This is delicious! Did you make it yourself?
quests.correctAnswer: This is so good! Did you make it from scratch?
acceptedSynonyms: Wow, this lasagna is incredible. Is it your own recipe?
It's fantastic. Did you cook it yourself?
This is so good! Did you make it from scratch?
This is really tasty. Where did you learn to cook like this?

quests.hint: Accept a compliment with thanks and add a personal touch. Don't argue with the praise.
quests.explanation: Many learners deny compliments ('No, it was bad'). In English, it's normal to say thank you, and a comment like 'I was nervous' makes you sound human.
quests.situationText: After a talk to your team, a colleague says, 'That presentation was really clear and well organized.' You were very nervous before it.
quests.sampleAnswer: Thank you, that means a lot. I was really nervous, so I'm glad it went well.
quests.correctAnswer: Thank you, that's very kind. I was quite nervous, so I'm glad it went well.
acceptedSynonyms: Thank you, that's very kind. I was quite nervous, so I'm glad it went well.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I was so nervous beforehand, so it's good to hear.
That's kind of you to say. I was worried it wouldn't go well.
Thank you! I put a lot of work into it, so I'm really pleased.

quests.hint: Compliment something the person can control, like a haircut, and say why it works.
quests.explanation: Compliments about choices, not personal features, feel comfortable. Adding 'it suits you' explains why you like it, which makes the compliment feel thoughtful.
quests.situationText: Your friend arrives at the cafe with a completely new short haircut. She looks different and happy.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, I love your new haircut! It really suits you.
quests.correctAnswer: I really like your new haircut. It suits you.
acceptedSynonyms: Your hair looks great short. It really suits you.
Wow, that new cut looks fantastic on you.
I really like your new haircut. It suits you.
New haircut? I love it. It looks really good on you.

quests.hint: State what you'd choose and why. 'I'd rather…' is a good way to state a preference.
quests.explanation: 'I'd rather' is a natural way to express a preference between two options. A short reason ('I'm too tired') helps friends understand your choice without a long discussion.
quests.situationText: Your friend can't choose between a comedy and a serious drama at the cinema. She asks which one you'd rather see. You had a long day and want to relax.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'd rather see the comedy, if that's okay. I'm too tired for something serious.
quests.correctAnswer: I'd rather see the comedy. I'm too tired for something serious.
acceptedSynonyms: Let's go for the comedy. I need something light after today.
The comedy for me, please. I don't think I can concentrate on a drama tonight.
I'd prefer the comedy. I've had a long day and I want to laugh.
I'd rather see the comedy. I'm too tired for something serious.

quests.hint: Compare two options and admit the trade-off. 'Even though' allows you to explain a choice with a downside.
quests.explanation: A preference feels honest when it admits a downside. 'Even if it costs more' shows you have considered both options.
quests.situationText: You're planning a trip and your friend asks whether you're taking the train or the bus. The train is faster and more comfortable but a bit more expensive.
quests.sampleAnswer: I prefer the train, because it's faster and more comfortable, even if it costs a bit more.
quests.correctAnswer: I prefer the train because it's faster and more comfortable, even though it costs a little more.
acceptedSynonyms: The train, definitely. It's quicker and nicer, although it's slightly more expensive.
I prefer the train because it's faster and more comfortable, even though it costs a little more.
I'd take the train. It costs more, but it's faster and more comfortable.
Probably the train. It's a bit pricier, but I like the comfort and the speed.

quests.hint: Answer with your choice, then a reason based on your own habits.
quests.explanation: Personal reasons ('I have more energy') make your answer feel real. They also let the other person find shared ground or an interesting difference.
quests.situationText: A friend wants to start going to the gym together and asks whether you prefer mornings or evenings.
quests.sampleAnswer: Mornings for me. I have more energy, and the gym is much quieter.
quests.correctAnswer: I prefer mornings. I have more energy, and the gym is quieter.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm better in the morning. I have more energy, and there are fewer people.
Mornings work better for me. I feel more awake, and it's less crowded.
Definitely mornings. By the evening I'm too tired, and it's busier.
I prefer mornings. I have more energy, and the gym is quieter.

quests.hint: Ask about what someone studies and follow with an opinion question. It turns a fact into a conversation.
quests.explanation: 'Do you like it?' is the natural follow-up that moves from a fact to an opinion. A single question is polite, but a pair shows real interest.
quests.situationText: In the first week of university, you sit next to a classmate you haven't met. You'd like to know more about her.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, what are you studying? Are you enjoying it so far?
quests.correctAnswer: What are you studying? Do you like it?
acceptedSynonyms: Which course are you doing? How are you finding it?
What are you studying? Do you like it?
What's your major? Are you enjoying it?
So what subject are you here for? Do you like it so far?

quests.hint: Questions about a visit are safe and friendly. Ask about duration and the first-time experience.
quests.explanation: Asking a visitor how long they're staying is a normal, friendly question that doesn't feel invasive. 'Is this your first time?' invites them to share their impressions.
quests.situationText: You're chatting with a foreign visitor at a friend's barbecue. He says he arrived a few days ago.
quests.sampleAnswer: How long will you be here for? Have you been to the city before?
quests.correctAnswer: How long are you staying here? Is this your first time in the city?
acceptedSynonyms: How long will you be here for? Have you been to the city before?
Are you here for long? Is it your first visit?
How many days do you have here? Is this your first trip to the city?
How long are you staying here? Is this your first time in the city?

quests.hint: Ask about someone's history in the area and tell them why you're asking. A reason makes it less like an interview.
quests.explanation: 'I'm still learning where everything is' explains your curiosity and invites them to give advice. It's a natural way to ask a personal question without feeling nosy.
quests.situationText: You've just moved into a new building and meet a neighbor while waiting for the lift. She looks like she has lived here a while.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, have you lived in this area long? I'm still finding my way around.
quests.correctAnswer: Have you lived around here for long? I'm still learning where everything is.
acceptedSynonyms: Have you been in this neighborhood for a while? I've only just moved in.
Have you lived around here for long? I'm still learning where everything is.
Do you know the area well? I'm new here and still working out where things are.
How long have you lived in the building? I only arrived last week.
